newsitem.title: USA: Japan's silence signals additional dlr/yen gains.
newsitem.headline: Japan's silence signals additional dlr/yen gains.

text.p: A conspicuous absence of yen-supportive comments from Japanese officials of late suggests Japan may be content to let fundamentals dictate a further weakening of its currency against the dollar, U.S. experts said on Monday.

With its stock market ailing, an austere budget plan due to take hold in early 1997, and lingering signs of economic weakness, Japan appears to have changed the tune it was singing as recently as November.

It was then, as the dollar approached 115 yen, that Eisuke Sakakibara, the influential Japanese Ministry of Finance (MOF) official, said he believed the dollar's correction from 1995 lows against the yen was about to end.
But now, with skepticism about Japan's economic recovery on the rise, Japanese officials have greeted a dramatic rise in the dollar's value against the yen with noticeable silence.

"Officialdom, whether it be the MOF or the Bank of Japan, had ample opportunity last night to make their displeasure known on dollar/yen," said Bob Near, vice president on the corporate foreign exchange desk at Bank of New York.
"They chose not to and that had to be a conscious decision," he added.
The dollar reached a peak of 116.20 yen on Friday, its highest level since late March of 1993. On Monday, it was hovering near the 116-even threshold for much of the session.

An increasingly uncertain outlook for Japan's economy and sliding stocks -- particularly in the troubled banking sector -- have strengthened the view that Tokyo will keep interest rates low to boost growth. This, in turn, has sent investors flocking to higher yielding currencies such as the dollar and the British pound.
Further compounding problems was last week's budget release. Tax revenues were estimated at 57.8 trillion yen for the coming fiscal year, up 12.6 percent from the current fiscal year's budget.

With the large increase -- mainly due to a two percentage point rise in the consumption tax -- and otherwise tight budget measures, investors are worried about the economy may not be able to get its head above water in 1997.
As a result, experts said, government officials are now finding it increasingly difficult to argue against further yen weakness.

"I think they're doing and saying things differently than they did a few months ago when they were trying to hold a top at 113 or 114 yen," said Andrew Hodge, vice president and financial strategist at Bank Brussels Lambert.
"And I think what happened recently and caused a shift in policy was renewed deflationary news for the Japanese economy," he added, referring to the fiscal package.
With foreign exchange dealing in Japan on hold for the holidays until January 6, currency traders said they would prefer to take a wait-and-see approach on dollar/yen.

Last week's surge to multi-year highs occurred in an extremely thin trading environment which exaggerated market moves. Therefore, where dollar/yen ends next week will give a clearer indication of just how far the rate can climb, dealers said.
Nevertheless, the market appears to agree that further upside is in store and that Japanese officials are unlikely to voice their displeasure at such a trend for the time being.

"I don't think you can expect the Japanese to be encouraging a weaker yen anymore but I think they are very much of the mindset that they've got to let the market fundamentals to go to work," said Stephen Flanagan, senior foreign exchange dealer at Credit Agricole. "The real fundamentals still argue for a weaker yen."
